question.explanation:
To find the slope at a given point, we have to find $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}$ at that point.

This question requires the product rule. Let $u(x) = \sin 2x$ and $v(x) =\cos 3x.$ Then

\[ u'(x) = 2\cos 2x, \qquad v'(x) = -3\sin 3x. \]

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u$ and $v.$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

\[ \eqalign{ \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} & = u'(x) \cdot v(x) + u(x) \cdot v'(x) \\[5pt] & = (2\cos 2x)\left( \cos 3x \right) + (\sin 2x)\left( -3\sin 3x \right)\\[5pt] & = 2\cos 2x \cos 3x - 3\sin 2x \sin 3x. } \]

Therefore, the slope at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is

\begin{align} \left.\left(\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}\right)\right|_{x=\pi/2} & = 2\cos\left( 2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \cos \left( 3\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - 3\sin \left( 2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \sin \left( 3\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\[5pt] & = 2\cos\left( \pi\right) \cos \left( \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) - 3\sin \left( \pi\right) \sin \left( \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) \\[5pt] & = 0 . \end{align}

example.title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Product Rules

question.explanation:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x) = e^{3x}$ and the denominator $v(x) = x^3+1.$

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

\[ u'(x) = 3e^{3x}, \qquad v'(x) = 3x^2. \]

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &= \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\left(3e^{3x}\right)(x^3+1) - (e^{3x})(3x^2)}{(x^3+1)^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {3(x^3+1)e^{3x} - 3x^2e^{3x}}{(x^3+1)^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {3((x^3+1) - x^2)e^{3x}}{(x^3+1)^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {3\left(x^3 - x^2 +1\right)e^{3x}}{\left(x^3+1\right)^2}. } \end{eqnarray}

example.title: Calculating a Derivative Using the Chain and Quotient Rules

question.explanation:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x) = x^3$ and the denominator $v(x) = \ln {(2x+1)}.$

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

\[ u'(x) = 3x^2, \qquad v'(x) = \dfrac{2}{2x+1}. \]

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $v.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &= \dfrac{u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x)\cdot v'(x)}{[v(x)]^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\left(3x^2\right)(\ln{(2x+1)}) - \left(x^3\right)\left(\dfrac{2}{2x+1}\right)}{\left( \ln {(2x+1)} \right)^2} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {3x^2\ln{(2x+1)} - \dfrac{2x^3}{2x+1}}{\left( \ln {(2x+1)} \right)^2}. } \end{eqnarray}
